enrichment.short_title: Break clause requiring vacant possession of shop units
key_facts: JIS leased an office building at One Legg Street, Chelmsford, with shop units included in the demised premises but subject to a back-underlease to the landlord when office use planning permission was refused.
Clause 5 gave the tenant an option to break the lease at the sixteenth year on giving vacant possession of the demised premises.
The tenant sought a declaration that vacant possession need not extend to the shop units, or rectification to exclude them from the break clause.
Hart J dismissed the construction claim and allowed the rectification claim to proceed; the Court of Appeal heard both issues together.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal on construction and rectification of a commercial lease break clause.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed with no order as to costs; construction claim failed but rectification may proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where a lease expressly defines demised premises to include shop units subject to an underlease, the break clause cannot be rewritten by construction simply because vacant possession is practically difficult; however, credible evidence of shared intention from both parties' witnesses may justify refusing summary dismissal of a rectification claim even where outward accord is disputed.
legal_issues: Construction of a tenant break clause requiring vacant possession
Correction of obvious drafting error as a matter of construction
Rectification for common mistake and the requirement of outward accord
Effect of underlease on exercise of a headlease break option

enrichment.short_title: Asylum claim after gang rape and trafficking fear

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: A Moldovan asylum seeker claimed she was gang raped in July 2001 and overheard her attackers arranging to traffic her to Turkey for prostitution before she escaped at a petrol station.
The adjudicator found her not credible in key respects but the IAT refused leave to appeal against her rejection of the trafficking-based social group claim.
The claimant remained in her village for about two weeks after the attack without being re-abducted and reported threatening phone calls to the police.
Hooper J reviewed whether the adjudicator was entitled to find no real risk the perpetrators would seek her out on return.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator accepts a claimant's account of a past kidnapping attempt but finds no reason to believe the same gang would seek her out if she returned, and that finding is supported by her remaining safely in the village for two weeks and police investigations, the conclusion is not irrational and Article 3 protection is not established.
legal_issues: Well-founded fear of persecution based on membership of a particular social group
Article 3 ECHR protection against trafficking and prostitution
Rationality of adverse credibility findings on risk of future harm
Adequacy of state protection in Moldova

enrichment.short_title: PAYE coding for anticipated Lloyd's underwriting losses
key_facts: Keeling, a Lloyd's Name, expected substantial underwriting losses for 2003/4 to be declared in May 2003.
He asked HMRC to amend his PAYE coding for 2002/3 to reflect anticipated loss relief against pension income.
General Commissioners allowed the coding appeal; the Revenue appealed by case stated.
The dispute was whether future loss relief could be taken into account before the loss was formally established under section 380 ICTA 1988.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from General Commissioners to the High Court on a point of law.
enrichment.outcome: Revenue appeal dismissed; PAYE coding may reflect anticipated future loss relief.
enrichment.ratio: The PAYE regime is a provisional assessment system distinct from the formal loss relief claim procedure; under regulation 7(2)(f) an Inspector may adjust a tax code to reflect future entitlements known at the time of coding, even where section 380 relief is not yet formally claimable.
legal_issues: Whether anticipated Lloyd's underwriting losses may be reflected in a PAYE code
Interaction between section 380 ICTA 1988 and the PAYE regulations
Construction of regulation 7(2)(a) and the sweeper provision in paragraph (f)
Timing of entitlement to loss relief for Names

enrichment.short_title: Certificate of operability notice in hotel development
key_facts: Embankment developed Blackfriars House into a Crowne Plaza hotel under a £28.14 million development agreement with Blackfriars.
Completion required both practical completion and a Certificate of Operability issued after inspections under schedule 2 paragraph 13.
Paragraph 13.1 required the developer to give the manager at least eight working weeks' notice of the date by which it would have complied with its obligations.
Embankment relied on letters of 4 January and 11 April 2002 as paragraph 13.1 notices; Forbes J held they were invalid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal of a declaration that valid paragraph 13.1 notices had been served.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; neither letter constituted a valid paragraph 13.1 notice.
enrichment.ratio: A paragraph 13.1 notice must specify the date, at least eight working weeks ahead, by which the developer anticipates compliance with its obligations so the manager can prepare to operate the hotel; a request to begin inspections or a notice of past compliance without a future date does not satisfy the clause even applying Mannai purposive construction.
legal_issues: Construction of contractual notice requirements
Whether a specific future date is required under paragraph 13.1
Application of Mannai principles to unilateral contractual notices
Distinction between notice under paragraph 13.1 and request under paragraph 13.2

enrichment.short_title: Liner conference dominance and predatory pricing claim
key_facts: Arkin, managing director of BCL Shipping Line, claimed damages for anticompetitive conduct by CONISCON and UKISCON liner conferences on UK/Continent-Israel container routes.
BCL entered the market in 1988 and withdrew in late 1991 after rate wars involving MSC and conference members.
The claim alleged abuse of dominance through predatory pricing, fighting ships and rumour spreading, and Article 81 infringements affecting block exemption.
Colman J held this was the first English damages claim under Article 82.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of a private damages claim for breach of Articles 81 and 82 EC.
enrichment.outcome: Claim failed on abuse, block exemption and causation; no damages awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Liner conferences may hold a collective dominant position in a defined container route market without abusing it where rate cuts lack eliminatory intent; even if breaches were found, BCL's losses were predominantly caused by its own decision to remain in the market at unsustainably low rates rather than by conference conduct.
legal_issues: Whether liner conferences constituted a collective dominant entity
Definition of the relevant product market for container liner services
Abuse of dominance through predatory pricing and fighting ships
Application of the liner conference block exemption under Article 81
Causation and quantification of competition damages

enrichment.short_title: VAT estimation dispute settled without costs order
key_facts: Littlewoods sought judicial review over Customs and Excise treatment of VAT estimation under regulation 29(3).
The parties reached a sensible settlement allowing Littlewoods to use estimation on a short-term basis before considering long-term approval.
Littlewoods argued Customs should pay costs because short-term approval had been considered internally in May 2002 without disclosure.
Moses J held Littlewoods persisted in seeking long-term approval even after learning short-term approval might be available.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review proceedings recalled for determination of costs after parties settled the substantive dispute.
enrichment.outcome: No order for costs; each party to bear its own costs including the costs hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties eventually settle a VAT estimation dispute through sensible negotiation after each kept its position during pre-litigation discussions, a fair costs order is no order as to costs rather than awarding costs against Customs for not disclosing internal consideration of short-term approval.
legal_issues: Costs following settlement of judicial review proceedings
Whether Customs should have disclosed internal consideration of short-term VAT estimation approval
Regulation 29(3) long-term versus short-term estimation

confidence.notes: Short costs-only judgment after settlement; substantive VAT issues not finally decided.

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid brief fee for copyright strike-out hearing
key_facts: Orwin brought a legally aided copyright infringement claim against British Coal relating to conveyor equipment drawings.
Counsel claimed a £15,500 brief fee for a strike-out application heard over several days in 2000-2001; the Deputy Costs Judge allowed £5,000.
Separate fees for chronology and skeleton argument were disallowed and treated as included in the brief fee.
Lawrence Collins J heard counsel's appeal against the reduced brief fee assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court against a detailed assessment decision on counsel's brief fee in legally aided proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: On appeal from a costs judge's assessment of a brief fee, the court will intervene only if the decision was wrong; where counsel spent about twelve days preparing for a one-day strike-out listing, a costs judge was entitled to find a £15,500 brief fee disproportionate and allow £5,000 including preparation for chronology and skeleton.
legal_issues: Standard of review on appeal from detailed costs assessment
Reasonableness and proportionality of counsel's brief fee
Whether chronology and skeleton work should be included in the brief fee
Use of opposing party's counsel fees as a yardstick in taxation

enrichment.short_title: Agency driver denied employee status at end-user
key_facts: Franks worked as a driver and later help-desk operator at Reuters through agency First Resort from 1993 until dismissal in 1999.
First Resort paid his wages and deducted PAYE; Reuters controlled his day-to-day work.
The employment tribunal found no mutuality of obligation between Franks and Reuters and held he was not their employee.
The EAT upheld that decision applying Carmichael v National Power on lack of mutuality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against employment tribunal and EAT decisions on preliminary issue of employee status.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to a fresh tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal cannot lawfully conclude that a worker is not an employee for lack of mutuality of obligation without first determining, on all relevant evidence including conduct and surrounding circumstances, whether there was an express or implied contract of service between the worker and the end-user.
legal_issues: Employee status of an agency worker placed with an end-user
Mutuality of obligation under Carmichael
Implied contract of service in tripartite agency arrangements
Relevance of length of placement and agency documentation

enrichment.short_title: Prostate cancer surgery side effects as progressive disability
key_facts: Kirton, a Tetrosyl employee in his late 50s, was diagnosed with asymptomatic prostate cancer and underwent radical prostatectomy in December 1999.
He suffered urinary incontinence as a post-operative side effect, which alone was not a substantial adverse effect on day-to-day activities.
The cancer was progressive and likely to spread within six to eight years, but the tribunals held the incontinence resulted from surgery not the cancer itself.
The Court of Appeal considered Schedule 1 paragraph 8 on progressive conditions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against Employment Appeal Tribunal decision on preliminary issue of disabled status.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claimant held to be a disabled person; matter remitted to the employment tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Under Schedule 1 paragraph 8 DDA 1995, an impairment resulting from standard surgical treatment for a progressive condition such as cancer may be treated as arising 'as a result of that condition' where the operation was the necessary medical response and the side effects are a routinely expected consequence.
legal_issues: Construction of 'as a result of that condition' in paragraph 8(1)(b)
Whether post-operative incontinence is linked to progressive prostate cancer
Trigger for protection under the progressive conditions provision
Distinction between condition symptoms and treatment side effects

enrichment.short_title: Parachute injury damages and police career multiplier
key_facts: Herring suffered serious spinal injuries in a 1994 Territorial Army SAS parachuting accident caused by the Ministry of Defence.
Before the accident he was a fit sports coach pursuing an HND in law with a strong prospect of joining the police.
The judge assessed future loss of earnings on a police career model, discounted the Ogden multiplier by 25%, and made pension and residual earnings awards.
The MoD appealed on multiplier methodology, residual earning capacity and post-retirement loss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against assessment of damages following liability admission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; future earnings loss increased by £59,300.
enrichment.ratio: Where a police career is used as a baseline earnings model because the claimant could likely earn equivalent sums elsewhere if that career did not materialise, it is wrong to apply an Allied Maples loss-of-chance percentage reduction for failing to join the police; contingency discounts should follow Ogden guidance and a 25% reduction was excessive on these facts.
legal_issues: Assessment of future loss of earnings for an unestablished career path
Loss of a chance versus conventional multiplier discount
Appropriate contingency discount under Ogden Tables
Smith v Manchester award for post-retirement labour market handicap
